blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — N95 respirator versus surgical mask
stem: Which statement best distinguishes a fit-tested N95 filtering facepiece respirator from a surgical mask in healthcare?

options.A: A fit-tested N95 is tight-fitting and filters at least 95% of airborne particles; a surgical mask is loose-fitting and lacks the same reliable aerosol protection.
options.B: A surgical mask is tight-fitting and requires fit testing for aerosol protection, while an N95 is loose-fitting and is used mainly as a fluid barrier.
options.C: Both devices provide equivalent aerosol respiratory protection when worn correctly, although the N95 is selected when greater splash resistance is needed.
options.D: An N95 provides particulate filtration without requiring a facial seal or fit testing, while a surgical mask relies on a tight seal for inhalation protection.

rationale: A is correct. Current CDC/NIOSH healthcare respiratory-protection guidance states that NIOSH Approved N95 filtering facepiece respirators tightly fit the face, require fit testing in a respiratory-protection program, and filter at least 95% of airborne particles. Surgical masks are loose-fitting and may block splashes and large droplets but do not provide a reliable level of protection from aerosolized particles because they do not form the same facial seal. B reverses the fit and purpose of the devices. C incorrectly treats their aerosol protection as equivalent. D incorrectly states that N95 respirators do not require a facial seal or fit testing and that surgical masks do.
educational_objective: Differentiate N95 respirators from surgical masks by recognizing the N95's tight facial seal, fit-testing requirement, and particulate respiratory protection.
